summary: Extends the Routing Information Protocol (RIP) so its messages carry more useful information and add a measure of security. It obsoletes RFC 1388. It has been replaced by RFC 2453.

plainLanguage.summary: RIP version 2 keeps the routing protocol that many small networks already use and adds the information the old format could not carry: the subnet mask for a route, the router to forward to, a tag marking where the route came from, and an optional password. It has since been replaced by RFC 2453.

questions: difference between rip v1 and rip v2
subtitle: RIP version 2 adds subnet masks, route tags, next hops and a password to the old RIP message format.

tldr.problem: The original RIP message could not carry a subnet mask, a next hop, the origin of a route or any authentication, so routers had to guess when a route did not fit a network.
tldr.mechanism: RIP version 2 keeps the same four octet header and 20 octet route entries, but fills each entry with an address family identifier, a route tag, the address, a subnet mask, a next hop and a metric. An optional password can occupy the first entry of a message.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1723 was an Internet Standard and updated RFC 1058. It has been obsoleted by RFC 2453.

today: RFC 1723 was an Internet Standard published in November 1994. It updated RFC 1058 and replaced RFC 1388, and it was later obsoleted by RFC 2453.

sections.title: Why Extend RIP
sections.content:
Routing Information Protocol (RIP) predates OSPF and IS-IS, and the RFC acknowledges that the newer interior gateway protocols are far superior. It argues that RIP still has advantages: in a small network it uses very little bandwidth and little configuration and management effort, and it is easy to implement compared with the newer protocols.

There are also many more RIP implementations in the field than OSPF and IS-IS combined, and the RFC expects that to remain true for some years. Because RIP will be useful for some time, it argues that making RIP more useful is worthwhile, especially since the gain is greater than the cost of the change.
sections.plainLanguage: Newer routing protocols are better, but RIP is simple, cheap and already widely deployed. This RFC adds a few fields to RIP instead of replacing it.

sections.title: What RIP Version 1 Could Not Say
sections.content:
The current RIP message holds the minimum information routers need to forward packets, and a large amount of unused space, because it was designed before several later ideas existed.

The protocol takes no account of autonomous systems, of the interaction between interior and exterior gateway protocols, of subnetting, or of authentication, because implementations of those postdate RIP. The missing subnet mask is the most serious problem: a router needs a subnet mask to determine a route. If a RIP route is a network route, with all non-network bits zero, the mask equals the network mask. If some of the non-network bits are set, the router cannot determine the subnet mask, and it cannot even tell whether the route is a subnet route or a host route. Some routers work around this by using the subnet mask of the interface on which the route was learned and deriving the route type from that.
sections.plainLanguage: The original RIP message had no subnet mask, so a router could not tell how much of an address is the network. It also said nothing about where a route came from and could not check who sent it.

sections.title: The RIP Version 2 Message Format
sections.content:
The RFC does not change RIP itself; it extends the message format. The first four octets of a RIP message hold the header, and the rest of the message is composed of 1 to 25 route entries of 20 octets each. All fields are coded in IP network byte order, which is big-endian.

The header holds a Command field, a Version field and two octets marked unused whose contents shall be ignored. The Version field is 2 for RIP messages that use authentication or carry information in any of the newly defined fields. Each route entry holds an Address Family Identifier, a Route Tag, an IP Address, a Subnet Mask, a Next Hop and a Metric.

The Route Tag is an attribute assigned to a route that must be preserved and readvertised with it. Its intended use is to separate internal routes, for networks within the RIP routing domain, from external routes, which may have been imported from an exterior gateway protocol or another interior gateway protocol. Routers that support other protocols should be configurable to set the tag on imported routes, either to an arbitrary value or at least to the number of the autonomous system the routes came from.

The Subnet Mask holds the mask that is applied to the IP address to yield the non-host portion of the address. If the field is zero, no subnet mask was included for that entry. On an interface where a RIP version 1 router may hear the information, three rules apply: information internal to one network must never be advertised into another network, information about a more specific subnet may not be advertised where RIP version 1 routers would consider it a host route, and supernet routes, whose netmask is less specific than the natural network mask, must not be advertised where RIP version 1 routers could misinterpret them.

The Next Hop is the address to which packets for the destination in that entry should be forwarded. A value of 0.0.0.0 means routing should be through the originator of the advertisement, and an address given as a next hop must be directly reachable on the logical subnet over which the advertisement is made. The field is advisory: if the information is ignored, a possibly sub-optimal but valid route may be taken, and a received next hop that is not directly reachable should be treated as 0.0.0.0.

Periodic broadcasts use the IP multicast address 224.0.0.9, which reduces the load on hosts that are not listening for RIP version 2 messages. IGMP is not needed, because these are inter-router messages that are not forwarded. A RIP version 2 router that receives a RIP version 1 Request should answer with a RIP version 1 Response, unless it is configured to send only RIP version 2 messages.
sections.plainLanguage: Each RIP version 2 message starts with a four byte header and then carries up to 25 route entries. Each entry now says which network the address belongs to, which router to forward to, and where the route came from.

sections.title: Authenticating a RIP Message
sections.content:
Authentication is a per-message function, and the only two octet field available in the message header are not enough for any reasonable authentication scheme. RIP version 2 therefore uses the space of an entire route entry: if the Address Family Identifier of the first, and only the first, entry in the message is 0xFFFF, the rest of that entry holds the authentication. Because one entry is used this way, at most 24 RIP entries can follow in the remainder of the message. If authentication is not in use, no entry in the message should have an Address Family Identifier of 0xFFFF.

The only authentication type defined here is simple password, which is type 2. The remaining 16 octets hold the plain text password, and a password shorter than 16 octets must be left-justified and padded on the right with nulls (0x00).

Section 4.2 gives the rules for what a receiver accepts. A router that is not configured to authenticate accepts RIP version 1 messages and unauthenticated RIP version 2 messages, and discards authenticated RIP version 2 messages. A router that is configured to authenticate accepts RIP version 1 messages and RIP version 2 messages that pass the authentication test, and discards unauthenticated messages and messages that fail the test. For maximum security, RIP version 1 messages should be ignored when authentication is in use.
sections.plainLanguage: A router can require a password on RIP version 2 messages. The password sits in the first route entry of the message, which leaves room for 16 characters. The password is sent in plain text, so it only stops routers that are not set up for it.

sections.title: Running Alongside RIP Version 1 Routers
sections.content:
RFC 1058 was careful about version numbers: RIP messages of version 0 are to be discarded, messages of version 1 are to be discarded if any Must Be Zero field is non-zero, and messages of any version greater than 1 should not be discarded simply because a Must Be Zero field holds a value other than zero. This means the new version of RIP is backwards compatible with existing RIP implementations that follow that rule.

A compatibility switch is still needed, for two reasons: some RIP version 1 implementations in the field do not follow RFC 1058, and multicasting would stop RIP version 1 systems from receiving RIP version 2 updates. The switch is configurable per interface and has four settings: RIP-1, where only RIP version 1 messages are sent; RIP-1 compatibility, where RIP version 2 messages are broadcast; RIP-2, where RIP version 2 messages are multicast; and none, which disables sending RIP messages. The recommended default is RIP-1 compatibility. Routers should also implement a receive control switch that determines whether to accept RIP version 1 only, RIP version 2 only, both, or none.

Two changes that were asked for were refused. A larger infinity, the value that marks a route as unreachable, cannot be used because it would break compatibility with older versions of RIP, which would at best ignore such a route. Making the Metric a single octet and reusing the high three octets would break implementations that treat the metric as a four octet entity. Addressless links, as in RIP version 1, are not supported by RIP version 2.
sections.plainLanguage: Old and new routers can share a network. A per-interface switch chooses whether to send only old messages, to broadcast new ones, to multicast new ones, or to send nothing. The default is to broadcast the new messages.

sections.title: What RIP Version 2 Does Not Secure
sections.content:
The RFC is blunt about the starting point: the basic RIP protocol is not a secure protocol. To bring RIP version 2 in line with more modern routing protocols, an extensible authentication mechanism has been incorporated into the protocol enhancements, and that mechanism is the one described in sections 3.1 and 4.2.

The mechanism that exists is a plain text password carried in the message, which means it identifies a sender to a receiver that already knows the password and nothing more. A sender can still advertise routes it should not, and the RFC does not add any protection against that.
sections.plainLanguage: RIP version 2 is not a secure protocol. The password it adds tells a router who sent a message, but it is only a check that the sender knows the password, and it travels in plain text.

data.title: RIP version 2 header and route entry

fields.name: Command
fields.desc: Request or response, as in RFC 1058.

fields.name: Version
fields.desc: Version number 2 for messages using authentication or any new field.

fields.name: Unused
fields.desc: Two octets whose contents shall be ignored.

fields.name: Address Family Identifier
fields.desc: Which kind of address the entry carries.

fields.name: Route Tag
fields.desc: Attribute preserved and readvertised with the route.

fields.name: IP Address
fields.desc: The destination address of the route.

fields.name: Subnet Mask
fields.desc: Mask applied to the address; zero means none was included.

fields.name: Next Hop
fields.desc: Router to forward to; 0.0.0.0 means the originator.

fields.name: Metric
fields.desc: Distance to the destination, as in RFC 1058.
